verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. The objects agree; the rewriting has two steps and one packaging choice. (i) Lean applies the primitive to the raw torus-averaged residual rather than to the paper's already-corrected bracket: `physicalBarSigma P e q f` unfolds through `sigma` to -R^{-e}·compactIntegral(cutoff P)(R^e ⟨f⟩_Y), which is the paper's -T_e⟨f⟩_Y (compactIntegral = pastIntegral − χ·totalIntegral is the paper's 𝓘_c = 𝓘 − χ_m𝒥 of (8.5)/(8.6), and `inversePower P e` equals r^{-e} on the shell, by inversePower_eq). The Lean theorem physicalSigma_eq_negative_primitive then converts this into -R^{-e}∫_0^R t^e (⟨f⟩_Y − b_e·mass_e⟨f⟩_Y) dt. The paper's H = -T_e(bracket) reaches the same expression because the bracket has zero weighted radial integral and is Y-independent, so its cutoff remainder 𝒜_e vanishes identically (last sentence of Lemma 8.2, p.90). (ii) The subtracted coefficient is written in Lean as the actual weighted moment mass_e⟨E⟩_Y, not as ε∂_Z𝒥_θ resp. ε∂_Z(𝒥_z + c_ρ𝒫); the two are identified by state_angular_moment and state_axial_moment, which are (8.16). The bump b_e = physicalDensity P e q is normalised by ∫r^e b_e = 1 exactly as σ_θ, σ_z are. The weights e = 2 for the θ row and e = 1 for the z row match T_2 and T_1. Lean's primitive carries no torus shift (compactIntegral is called with M = 0, v = 0): harmless here, since it is applied to the torus average, which no longer has a Y argument.
